Case Information: A 2-month-old male infant presented with a mass in the right lower limb, noted since birth and progressively enlarging. The mass measured approximately 5 × 5 cm, with a purplish-red discoloration and surrounding tissue swelling. The infant's past medical history, personal history, and immunization status were normal. There were no episodes of cyanosis, convulsions, or bleeding postnatally. Family history was negative for congenital malformations, tumors, or hemorrhagic conditions. On examination, the infant's vital signs were stable, and he was alert. Hemorrhagic spots were noted on the upper hard palate. A 5 × 5 cm mass was present at the right knee joint, which was warm to the touch, of medium consistency, and well-defined. No abnormalities were detected in the central nervous, cardiovascular, or respiratory systems.
Diagnostic Tests: The blood tests showed a moderate anemia (HGB 77 g/L) and severe thrombocytopenia (PLT 18 ​× ​109/L). The coagulation function showed prolonged clotting time (PT ​> ​120 s, reference, 10.0–16.0 s; APTT 45.1 s, reference, 20.0–40.0 s; TT 31 s, reference, 14.0–21.0 s) and significantly hypofibrinogenaemia (FBG 0.541 g/L, reference, 1.8–4.0 g/L). The coagulation profile was deranged with prolonged prothrombin (international normalized ratio [INR] out of range), activated partial thromboplastin time (prolonged >120 s above control) and elevated D-dimer levels (21.29 mg/dL, reference <0.55 mg/dL). Fibrinogen levels decreased (54.1 mg/dL, reference 180–400 mg/dL). The mass showed an iso-intense signal on T1 weighted image (T1WI) and an iso-to-mild intense signal on T2 weighted image (T2WI) in the subcutaneous fat layer of the inguinal region of the right thigh. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated multiple heterogeneous intense enhancement.

Case Information: A 54-year-old Caucasian male presented with abdominal pain and bloating, for which he had been using nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). His medical history includes hypertension, Raynaud’s syndrome, rectal cancer in remission post-surgical resection and radiation therapy, and ongoing radiation-induced cystitis. Two months prior, he was diagnosed with strongly positive anti-RNA polymerase III systemic sclerosis following the onset of dysphagia and was prescribed methotrexate (MTX) up to a dose of 20 mg weekly. He had not taken MTX for 14 days due to feeling unwell. Examination revealed a small bladder rupture attributed to cystitis, which did not necessitate surgical intervention. During the bladder evaluation, abnormal serum sodium and creatinine levels were detected, leading to further cardiac assessment.
Diagnostic Tests: A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a severely reduced left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction of 10%. A coronary catheterization demonstrated no significant coronary disease. A cardiac biopsy showed cardiac necrosis without evidence of inflammation or fibrosis.

Case Information: A 59-year-old, right-handed female with 12 years of education presented with a 2-year history of difficulty understanding spoken language. She had a background of well-controlled hypertension for 5 years. The patient reported that spoken conversation sounded like noise or buzzing, especially in crowded areas. She could not understand spoken questions during the interview but could comprehend and respond correctly through lip reading or gestural cues. She struggled to understand television dialogue but could follow foreign movies with Korean subtitles without issue. Environmental noises like doorbells and ringing phones were perceived and responded to appropriately. Her family noted no issues with her ability to express thoughts, recall events, navigate directions, or use public transportation. She managed household tasks, financial matters, and social activities without difficulty. A hearing aid prescribed by an otolaryngology clinic did not improve her comprehension. One year after symptom onset, she began making errors in simple mathematics and her spoken language comprehension declined significantly, though she could still read and write. Her writing style became rough with frequent spelling errors. She occasionally forgot things but it did not impact daily life. She had trouble recalling names of familiar neighbors but recognized them visually. Her demeanor and personal relationships remained unaffected. On examination, she scored 17 out of 30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination, with specific deficits in calculation, recall, and language. Neurological examination was unremarkable except for mild rigidity in the right upper extremity. The Korean version of the Western Aphasia Battery showed fluent spontaneous speech with phonemic paraphasia and mild neurogenic stuttering. Severe impairments were noted in comprehension and repetition, with mild impairments in visual confrontational naming and word generation. She could read aloud and understand written words and sentences, and communicate in writing with some literal errors. Audiological examination revealed mild bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with pure-tone thresholds of 30 dB in the left ear and 35 dB in the right ear within the 500-2,000 Hz range. Speech audiometry thresholds were 50 dB in the left ear and 60 dB in the right ear, with speech discrimination abilities of 32% at 80 dB in the left ear and 20% at 85 dB in the right ear. Brainstem auditory evoked potential responses were normal. She recognized six out of eight nonverbal animal sounds and correctly matched four out of six songs to their written titles. Neuropsychological test instructions were given in written form. She performed below normal on the Korean version of the Boston Naming Test, ideomotor praxis, Rey figure-copying test, calculation, finger naming, and the semantic subtest of the controlled oral association word recall test. In a Navon figure task, she recognized only small letters, indicating simultanagnosia. She had difficulty naming famous people but could describe the occupations of some she could not name. Routine laboratory tests showed no evidence of comorbid disease.
Diagnostic Tests: [11C] PIB-PET revealed elevated PIB binding in diffuse cortical areas, especially in the temporoparieto-occipital cortices. 18FDG-PET scan revealed hypometabolism in bilateral temporoparietal areas, with greater effects on the left. Brain MRI demonstrated mild atrophy in both temporal lobes, with the left side more affected.

Case Information: A 53-year-old male presented with multiple, dusky reddish nodules on the trunk, persisting for 7 years. These lesions were bilaterally distributed along the lateral sides of the trunk and had shown slight progression. The patient has a medical history of arterial hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. There were no systemic symptoms indicating involvement of other organs. The patient did not report any specific triggers causing induction or exacerbation of symptoms. Stroking the lesions resulted in swelling, itching, and redness of the skin.
Diagnostic Tests: Histological findings of the biopsy specimen showed nodular to diffuse dermal infiltration of lymphocytes with irregular nuclei, eosinophils, plasma cells, and mast cells. Kappa light chain restriction was suggested in the immunostaining results of the immunoglobulin (Ig) light chain. CD20 staining, a B-cell marker, revealed reactive lymphoid follicles with patch positivity. Periphery of lymphoid follicles showed BCL-2 positivity and BCL-6 positivity focally at the center. Toluidine blue and CD117 staining showed positivity, and several mast cells were confirmed. MUM1 and CD138 showed diffuse positivity and confirmed positive reaction in plasma cells. The Ig heavy chain gene rearrangement result showed B-cell monoclonality. Of the Igs measured in serum, only the IgG level was elevated to 1905.80 mg/dL. Peripheral blood smear and immunofixation electrophoresis results in serum and urine showed no abnormality. The patient did not show any evidence of hypermetabolic metastasis on whole body positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT).

Case Information: A 43-year-old man visited the outpatient endocrine clinic at Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Tabriz, Iran, accompanied by his sister, for an assessment of skin lesions. The patient exhibited multiple lesions on his shoulders, back, the lateral and medial parts of the dorsal surface of his feet, the medial and lateral malleus of both feet, and the dorsal and palmar surfaces of both hands. His siblings have been monitored in the same clinic for similar skin conditions. These conditions were characterized by palmar, eruptive, tuberous, and trauma site xanthomas, along with elevated levels of both total cholesterol and triglycerides in the plasma. Both parents had normal serum lipid levels. There was no history of coronary artery or other atherosclerotic disorders in the patient or his siblings. The patient reported no other complaints and maintained an active lifestyle as a greengrocer. A pathology report from a skin lesion biopsy performed by a dermatologist a few months prior indicated the presence of lipid-laden macrophages.
Diagnostic Tests: Fasting serum lipid levels reported as: Total cholesterol = 507 mg/dl, Triglycerides = 470 mg/dl and High Density Lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol = 41 mg/dl.

Case Information: A 19-year-old female presented to the emergency room with left-sided chest pain and cough. CT imaging identified multiple pulmonary emboli in the left inferior segmental pulmonary arteries. She had no provoking factors or other complications at that time and was discharged on rivaroxaban with hemoglobin at 14.9 g/dL and platelet count at 402 per uL. Six weeks later, she returned with right lateral chest wall pain and shortness of breath. Her hemoglobin was 6.6 g/dL and platelet count was 485 per uL. The patient reported developing menorrhagia after starting rivaroxaban. CT imaging showed a new pulmonary embolism in the right lower lobe segmental pulmonary arteries and a decreased clot burden in the left inferior segmental pulmonary artery branches. She received a packed red blood cell transfusion and was started on a heparin drip. There were no signs of heart failure or hypoxia, and she was started on norethindrone for menses suppression. Further laboratory tests showed ferritin at 6.8 ng/mL, and she received an iron transfusion. She was transitioned to warfarin and followed up one month later with hemoglobin at 10.8 g/dL, ferritin at 36.1 ng/mL, iron saturation at 25%, and platelet count at 566 per uL. A hypercoagulable workup including protein C, protein S, antithrombin III, factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutations, lupus anticoagulant, cardiolipin antibodies, and beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies was unrevealing. Persistent thrombocytosis and a report that the patient’s father was being treated for a similar condition led to testing for JAK2, MPL, CALR, and JAK2 exon 12-15 mutations, which were all negative. Subsequent CSA revealed a heterozygous variant of unknown significance with the genomic change Chr1(GRCh37):g.43805172C>A, predicted to result in a single amino acid substitution of glutamine to lysine at codon 208 in exon 4 of the MPL gene. This variant had not been reported as associated with a clinical condition according to the HGMD.
Diagnostic Tests: Bone marrow biopsy revealed normocellular marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis and mild megakaryocytic hyperplasia without atypia nor dysplasia.

Case Information: A 10-year-old female from a rural area in Kendrapada district, Odisha, presented to the pediatrics outpatient department with intermittent abdominal pain, anal itching, and restlessness at night for the past 2-3 weeks. Physical examination revealed no notable findings. Blood and urine tests showed no abnormalities. Her height was recorded at 130 cm and her weight at 29 kg.
Diagnostic Tests: Examination of the stool samples revealed spherical eggs 70 µm in diameter, yellow-colored, thick-shelled eggs that contained six central hooklets but no polar filaments. Further confirmation was done by examination of another stool sample by the concentration method. Again, the same findings were noted.

Case Information: An 80-year-old woman presented with difficulty in raising her right upper limb, progressive dyskinesia, and gait disorder. She had experienced neck pain for approximately 2 years and numbness in her extremities for about a year, both of which had worsened significantly before her visit. She could walk unassisted for less than 100 meters. Muscle weakness (manual muscle testing [MMT] score: 3) was observed in the entire right upper limb, while strength in the remaining limbs was normal. Hypesthesia was noted throughout the upper and lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were increased bilaterally in all limbs, with positive Hoffman’s and Wartenberg’s signs. Her preoperative Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score was 8.5 points. Radiographs and cervical contrast CT revealed osteolytic lesions in C3–7. A mass extended into the spinal canal from within the vertebrae, compressing the cervical spinal cord from the right side. The mass was stained in the early contrast phase and showed an internal low-density area. MRI detected a mass with the same signal profile as bone from within the C3–7 vertebrae to outside of the vertebral bodies, compressing the cervical spinal cord from the right side at the same levels. Blood tests showed no thrombocytopenia, anemia, or coagulation abnormalities. The inflammatory response was normal. Blood cultures and various tumor markers were negative. A percutaneous vertebral biopsy showed culture negativity and no neoplastic lesions.
Diagnostic Tests: The resected specimen exhibited various and complex proliferating patterns of vasoforming cells in low-magnification images, with most areas showing a combination of solid and vasodilated proliferating patterns. In solid areas, numerous vascular cavities had been formed by atypical cells, including epithelioid cells with infrequent mitosis. In the periphery, irregular nodules had infiltrated into the adjacent muscular and fatty-fibrous tissue. The nodules had a slit-like structure with spindle cells. Several nodules contained epithelioid cell proliferation that clearly showed ERG, CD31, and CD34, but not D2–40, immunopositivity, which were surrounded by cells positive for the pericytic markers myo1B, CD146, and SMA. The proliferating cells were negative for markers of epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, including CAMTA1, TFE3, and FOSB. The Ki-67 labelling index was calculated as approximately 16.1% (109/678) in areas with solid components and dilated capillaries and 10.6% (83/783) in areas containing slit-like blood vessels in the solid components.

Case Information: On March 7, 2018, a 35-year-old Chinese female presented with a one-year history of persistent erythematous papules and infiltrative plaques on the nose without any obvious triggers. Initially, a hard nodule the size of rice grains appeared on the right alar part of the nose, which was painless and itchy. Over time, the skin lesions gradually increased in size, became thick, and spread across the entire nose. Infiltrating plaques also developed on the upper jaw. Past and family history revealed no similar diseases within the family. Since the onset of the illness, the patient’s urine, stool, and weight remained normal. Skin examination revealed diffuse erythematous papules, infiltrations, and hypertrophic plaques on the entire nose and upper jaw, with a smooth surface. Dermoscopy showed a bright red background with diffuse telangiectasia, but no obvious keratinized hair follicle structures. Laboratory examinations, including antinuclear antibody, anti-dsDNA antibody, anti-Ro, anti-La, and Borrelia, as well as direct immunofluorescence serology, yielded negative results. Blood and urine routine tests, liver and kidney function tests, chest X-ray, and ECG all showed no obvious abnormalities. Maxillary CT plain scan with enhancement revealed several findings: (1) a soft tissue nodule in the right soft palate, with multiple enlarged lymph nodes in both necks, and thickening and enhancement of nasal soft tissue; (2) right frontal sinus and ethmoid sinusitis.
Diagnostic Tests: Histopathological examination of the biopsy sample showed a normal epidermis and an inflammatory infiltrate consisting of dense perivascular lymphocytes, as well as lymphocytes surrounding hair follicles and sweat glands in the dermis. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated a predominance of CD4+ T cells compared to CD8+ T cells. The immunohistochemical panel further revealed positive staining for CD3, CD4, CD8, CD20, CD43, CD68, CD1a, and Ki-67 (10%), while staining for CD123, CD56, GB, PAS, and acid-fast organisms was negative. TCR gene rearrangement analysis did not show any clonal amplification peaks in the target fragment.

Case Information: A 32-year-old woman reported experiencing painless unilateral blurring of vision in her left eye for the past three months. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/250 in the left eye. Examination of the right eye was normal with a cup disc ratio (CDR) of 0.5. The left eye showed engorged episcleral vessels, a relative afferent pupillary defect, grade III nuclear sclerosis with cortical cataract, and a CDR of 0.9 on fundus examination. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 16 mmHg in the right eye and 42 mmHg in the left eye, as measured by Goldman applanation tonometry. Gonioscopy indicated open angles in both eyes. There was no proptosis or audible bruit, and extraocular movements were full. Color vision and Humphrey visual field analysis 24-2 were normal in the right eye, while the left eye exhibited severely depressed fields with central 10° around fixation preserved. Treatment for the left eye included topical timolol maleate 0.5%, dorzolamide 2%, and travoprost 0.004%, along with systemic acetazolamide 250 mg twice daily.
Diagnostic Tests: Neuro-imaging showed no evidence of tumor, thrombosis, or arterio-venous malformations.

Case Information: A 14-year-old male, weighing 45 kg, was transferred to our clinic for further evaluation after being found to have pericardial effusion at a provincial hospital. Initial symptoms included fever and left shoulder pain. Physical examination revealed a reduction in the intensity of cardiac sounds and an elevated heart rate. Notably, the patient did not exhibit arthralgia or abdominal pain at any point during the clinical course. Three weeks before this event, the patient had an upper respiratory tract infection, which was treated with ibuprofen.
Diagnostic Tests: Echocardiography revealed a moderate pericardial effusion and a mild bilateral pleural effusion. Biological investigations showed the white blood cell count was 19,670/µL, the neutrophils count was 16.8/µL, the lymphocytes count was 810/µL, and there were high levels of inflammatory markers in the plasma tests: the C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 131 mg/L, the erythrocytes sedimentation rate (ESR) was 72 mm/h, the rheumatoid factor was positive (20UI/mL, normal value, NV < 14 UI/mL), and the ferritin level was high at 380.3 ng/mL (NV = 14–152 ng/mL). The complement fractions (C3, C4) were normal; autoantibodies were not detected; and the Quantiferon TB Gold, tuberculin skin test, and antibody work-up for common viral infections were all negative. An immunogram showed hypoIgG (652 mg/dL, NV 720–1700 mg/dL). Echocardiography revealed a circumferential pericardial effusion of 9–15 mm. Furthermore, a left pleural effusion was associated. The ECG showed PR segment depression and ST elevation in the inferior leads. In addition to a negative antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) profile, a Sanger sequencing for the MEFV gene was performed without any mutations identified. Biological investigations showed an elevated interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) level in the patient’s blood, with a 10 pg/mL recorded value (normal values < 5 pg/mL). Next-generation sequencing (NGS) performed by the Invitae Corporation, San Francisco, USA, revealed a previously unreported de novo missense mutation in the NLRP12 gene (c.1264G > A).

Case Information: A 5-day-old male neonate presented with widespread jaundice. He was born at term via vaginal delivery, weighing approximately 2100 g. The mother, with a history of six pregnancies and six live births, was generally healthy except for mild photosensitivity. The neonate had no history of clay-colored stools, fever, or drug administration. On admission, physical examination showed pale conjunctiva, yellowing of the sclera, generalized jaundice, a few red lesions around the eyes, and mild enlargement of the spleen. The pulse was irregular, with a heart rate of about 75 beats per minute. An electrocardiogram indicated third-degree atrioventricular block, while echocardiography revealed a patent foramen ovale without other abnormalities. Blood tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL) and low platelet count (80,000/mm3). A blood smear indicated erythrocyte hypochromia, anisocytosis, and poikilocytosis. The reticulocyte index, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were within normal ranges. Liver function tests were elevated: aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 760 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 187 U/L, alkaline phosphatase at 2045 U/L, total bilirubin at 12.4 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin at 6.2 mg/dL. Prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time were normal. TORCH titers, viral hepatitis markers, and thyroid function tests were normal. Blood and urine cultures for both mother and neonate were negative. Tests for metabolic diseases, including galactosemia, tyrosinemia, and phenylketonuria, were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal-sized liver and gall bladder, no bile duct dilation, and no biliary sludge. The spleen was mildly enlarged but had a normal echo pattern. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy indicated decreased hepatic uptake with no passage through the intrahepatic bile ducts. Initially, the skin lesions were a few non-scarring red annular plaques around the eyes. Over the next few days, these lesions spread to the nasal bridge and upper cheeks, developing sharp and slightly hyperkeratotic borders.
Diagnostic Tests: Serologic studies of the infant and mother were positive for antinuclear antibodies (ANA; 1: 640), anti-Ro/SSA: >4 index (normal: <1 index) and anti-La/SSB antibodies: >4 index (normal: <1 index).

Case Information: A one-day-old male infant, born at term with a birth weight of 3.1 kg, presented with no significant prenatal history and an uncomplicated delivery. Since birth, the infant had not passed stool and exhibited increased bilious vomiting and abdominal swelling. The anus was observed to be in a normal position with well-developed gluteal muscles and skin folds. The genital examination showed normally developed male genitalia with no visible signs of a fistula. The urine was clear and free from meconium contamination. A catheter could not be inserted more than half an inch into the anal opening. Imaging studies, including an echocardiogram, renal ultrasound, and vertebral X-ray, showed normal results with no indications of VACTERL association. An abdominal X-ray revealed multiple dilated bowel loops, including an S-shaped dilated loop of bowel extending downward toward the pelvis, indicative of the sigmoid colon.
Diagnostic Tests: Lower gastrointestinal fluoroscopy showed no contrast passage through the rectum, and the catheter tip met resistance at half an inch from the anal orifice.

Case Information: A 32-year-old adequately nourished male was admitted with complaints of shortness of breath for 1 month, which had worsened over the past 2 days. He had no other accompanying symptoms. The patient, who worked as a tailor and consumed a mixed diet, was found to be well-built and nourished with a body mass index of 25.3 kg/m2. On examination, he was tachypneic, had tachycardia, and a mild fever. Oral thrush was observed, and scrapings were sent for fungal culture. There were no apparent risk factors for immunosuppressive states. A chest X-ray showed scattered inspiratory crackles, and his SpO2 was 87%. High flow oxygen was initiated, and he was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit for further management. Blood gas analysis revealed a PO2 of 47 mmHg and a PCO2 of 24 mmHg. A chest roentgenogram showed bilateral perihilar infiltrates. Empirical antibiotics, fluconazole, and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) were started along with steroids. Lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 916 U/L, and high-resolution computed tomography of the thorax showed ground glass opacities in both lung fields, predominantly perihilar. Other routine blood work was normal. The patient remained tachypneic on high flow oxygen and intermittently required noninvasive ventilation. Bronchoalveolar lavage revealed pneumocystis organisms. Acid-fast bacteria and routine bacterial and fungal cultures were negative. The fungal scrapings grew Candida albicans, which was sensitive to fluconazole. HIV ELISA tests were negative on two separate occasions. Western blot and HIV-RNA polymerase chain reaction tests were also negative.
Diagnostic Tests: The CD4 turned out to be 110/mm3 and the CD4% was 14.3. The CD8 counts were 312/mm3 with a CD4:CD8 ratio, inverted (0.35; normal: 1.4–1.7). This test was repeated after 6 weeks and the results were the same.

Case Information: A 17-year-old female presented with a 7-month history of intermittent swelling in the lower extremities, protein in the urine, and blood in the urine. A renal biopsy conducted at another hospital 4 months prior suggested possible IgA nephropathy, and she was treated with the angiotensin receptor blocker valsartan, but her symptoms persisted. She had no history of drug use, infections, malignancy, or family history of hepatitis B or C, HIV, rheumatic disease, or tumors. She was normotensive, and both general physical and funduscopic examinations were normal. Her lung fields were clear without rales or fremitus. A 24-hour urine protein test showed a total protein level of 2.75 g. Urinalysis revealed 24 erythrocytes per high-power field. Serum levels of urea, creatinine, and albumin were within normal ranges. Autoantibody tests were unremarkable, and serum antiphospholipase A2 receptor antibodies were negative. Renal ultrasound findings were normal. A review of the previous renal biopsy showed 22 glomeruli, with 1 (4.5%) showing global sclerosis and 1 (4.5%) showing focal segmental sclerosis. There was mild mesangial expansion, thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, endothelial swelling, focally swollen podocytes, and hypercellularity. Swelling of the tubular epithelium and patchy infiltration of lymphocytes and monocytes in the interstitial area were noted, without interstitial fibrosis. The capillary walls in the interstitial area showed no lesions. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed granular deposits along the capillary walls for IgM, C3, C1q, and kappa and lambda light chains, with mild staining for IgG and IgA. IgG subclass staining showed segmental positivity for IgG1 but negativity for IgG2, IgG3, IgG4, and antiphospholipase A2 receptor. Granular deposits along the capillary walls, especially for lambda and C1q, indicated immune complexes. Silver staining showed spike-like projections at the 3-o'clock position, indicating a spiked glomerular basement membrane around the immune complexes. Masson staining showed scattered fuchsinophilic deposits, indicating immune complexes. The lesions of mesangial cells, endothelial cells, and podocytes were noted. Lupus nephritis was excluded due to the absence of systemic lupus manifestations and negative immunoserological markers except for an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:100. No solid tumors or hematological malignancies were detected by computed tomography or hematological examinations, and all tumor biomarkers were negative.
Diagnostic Tests: Genetic testing revealed compound heterozygous mutations of MMACHC (NM_015506). The proband was a compound heterozygote for two transitions: one in exon 1 (chr1:45966084, c.80A>G) and the other in exon 4 (chr1:45974520, c.482G>A) of MMACHC. These predicted p.Gln27Arg and p.Arg161Gln missense changes at the amino acid level.

Case Information: A 26-year-old male visited Tianjin Medical University General Hospital due to a painless neck lump, first noticed 6 years ago, which had recently grown rapidly. The patient experienced agitation, irritability, excessive sweating, and discomfort while swallowing. Previously, he had been diagnosed with nodular goiter by other hospitals and had intermittently taken Euthyrox® for several years. He also reported childhood hearing impairment and language learning difficulties, though clinical examination indicated normal mental and physical development. Physical examination revealed a visible grade III goiter, with an enlarged, tough thyroid without palpable nodules and a clear boundary. Laboratory tests showed a free thyroxine level of 9.99 pmol/l (normal range: 11.5–23.5 pmol/l), a free triiodothyronine level of 6.07 pmol/l (normal range: 3.5–6.5 pmol/l), and a thyroid stimulating hormone level of 2.401 μlU/ml (normal range: 0.3–5.0 μlU/ml). Thyrotrophin receptor, thyroglobulin, thyroperoxidase antibodies, carcinoembryonic antigen, thyroglobulin, and calcitonin levels were within normal ranges. A chest X-ray showed tracheal narrowing at the superior thoracic aperture, and a thyroid ultrasound revealed multiple hypoechoic signals in each lobe and isthmus of the thyroid. Cervical lymph node enlargement was also noted. Cervical computed tomography scan showed diffuse enlargement of each lobe and thickening of the thyroid isthmus, with numerous oval, low- and slightly high-density nodules in the thyroid. Electrical capacitance tomography results were consistent with signs of a nodular goiter.
Diagnostic Tests: The two vestibular aqueducts were enlarged, more markedly in the right aqueduct.

Case Information: A 49-year-old male was admitted in July 2010 due to sudden onset of weakness in the proximal muscles of his limbs, affecting both sensory and motor functions. Upon clinical examination, he exhibited muscle weakness in the proximal regions of both upper and lower limbs, accompanied by sensations of tingling and pain. The muscle stretch reflexes in his lower limbs were reduced. There were no signs of upper motor neuron involvement. Nerve conduction studies showed normal results.
Diagnostic Tests: Needle electromyography showed abnormal spontaneous activity and neurogenic recruitment in weak muscles. Anti-HEV IgM was detected in serum (optical density ratio >10) but not in CSF. HEV RNA was detected by real-time PCR only in serum (Ct 34).

Case Information: An 8-year-old girl from a rural area presented with pain in her left leg and an ulcer on the anterior aspect of her left shin, persisting for 15 days. These symptoms have been recurring over the past 4 years. The ulcer typically healed with antibiotics but reappeared after a few days. A biopsy from the ulcer indicated chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Imaging showed no signs of osteomyelitis. She received anti-tubercular therapy followed by multidrug therapy for leprosy, but the ulcer continued to recur. On physical examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm ulcer on the anterior aspect of the shin and a healed ulcer just above the current one. Sensation was intact, and there were no thickened nerves or lymphadenopathy. Her general and systemic examinations, as well as laboratory investigations, were within normal limits.
Diagnostic Tests: A X-ray of left leg showed no evidence of osteomyelitis however, it revealed a linear calcification ending in the ulcer. Previous X-ray also showed the same linear calcification.

Case Information: A 72-year-old woman experienced behavioural changes, unsteadiness, and frequent falls over the past year. She had started oral anticoagulant therapy two years earlier due to paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Relatives reported that over the past year, she became more listless and neglected work and domestic activities. She also exhibited hyperreligious behaviour, anxiety, loss of appetite, mild lower limb weakness, and falls. Subsequently, she experienced periods of agitation, confusion, and visual hallucinations, leading to the initiation of antipsychotic medication. Her condition worsened, resulting in the loss of her ability to walk and confinement to a wheelchair. Upon admission, she showed disorientation, apathy, apraxia, short-term memory deficit (MMSE = 7), anosmia, mild flaccid proximal paraparesis, and muscular atrophy. Patellar reflexes and plantar responses were normal. Urinary incontinence was present, but there were no signs of sensory impairment. A comprehensive workup, including vitamin levels, thyroid function, and tumour markers, was normal. A 24-hour Holter monitor test revealed no paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. EEG indicated patterns of diffuse cerebral dysfunction without epileptic activity. A full-body CT scan and a breast ultrasound were unremarkable.
Diagnostic Tests: A brain MRI revealed T2*-pondered hypointensities around cerebral cortex (with a bilateral frontotemporal and insular predominance) and around the brainstem suggesting deposition of iron-containing products. An angioMRI did not reveal any source of bleeding. Spinal MRI showed T2* pondered hypointensities all along the spinal cord with thecal iron accumulation between L4 and S1. There were also signs of arachnoiditis between L2 and L4. CSF analysis revealed xanthochromia, 4500 red blood cells (RBC)/μL, 61 mg/dL in proteic concentration, and normal glucose level. CSF VDRL was negative and there were no neoplastic cells.

Case Information: A 21-month-old male presented to the emergency department with respiratory symptoms. Over the past 10 months, there has been a noted increase in penile size and skin darkening. A sibling passed away 13 years ago with similar symptoms. The patient's weight was 13 kg (Z-score: 1.1, 85.3th percentile), height was 92 cm (Z-score: 2.4, 99.2th percentile), and blood pressure was 139/90 mmHg (Z-score for age-based pediatric blood pressure for systolic/diastolic pressure: 4.3/3.9, 100th percentile. Z-score equal to or greater than 95th percentile indicates hypertension). Physical examination revealed hyperpigmentation of the gums, skin, and scrotum, facial acne, and penile enlargement measuring 8.7 cm (above 90th percentile). Testicular size was prepubertal (less than 2 mL) with no pubic hair.
Diagnostic Tests: Laboratory tests showed serum ACTH: 507 pg/mL (normal: 5–60 pg/mL), cortisol: 44 μg/dL (normal: 55–248 μg/dL), 17α-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP): 67 nmol/L (normal: 0.3–2.5 nmol/L), DOC: 319 ng/dL (normal: 4–49 ng/dL), and androstenedione: 11 ng/mL (normal: 0.4–4.1 ng/mL).
